articles.text: It is the anniversary of the most difficult, most peculiar, and most isolated year of our lifetimes. On March 16, 2020, Piedmont’s City Council officially declared a local emergency in an effort to address growing concerns over a novel virus spreading throughout the world. It would be city council’s last in-person meeting. The item to adopt a resolution ratifying proclamation of local emergency was not originally included in the March 16, 2020 agenda but was added by City Administrator Sara Lillevand hours before the meeting. At the time, Gov. Gavin Newsom suspended the provisions of the Brown Act, which would have required advance notice of the agenda change. Every other seat in the council chambers was taped off to adhere to a newfangled rule that would soon become second nature to us. A six-foot distance between individuals was required, and by the next council meeting, all members would meet via teleconference application “Zoom.” From the beginning, Piedmont stayed in line with Alameda County Public Health Department orders; businesses deemed “non-essential” were forced to close, and residents were asked to stay home. A sign posted on City Hall read that it would be “closed to public access for all non-essential business, March 16 through March 29.” The limitation is still in place one year later. Similarly, the school district announced the closure of all schools until March 27, 2020. That decision was made on a Friday afternoon, March 13, with both Supt. Randy Booker and then-School Board President Amal Smith agreeing that it was in the best interest of students’ and faculty’s health. Meanwhile, both San Francisco and Alameda counties announced school closures throughout their respective districts for three weeks, from March 16 through April 3. A slew of event cancellations followed or were soon adapted to digital platforms. Some companies and organizations held on to optimism and declared events “postponed.” The 2020 Summer Olympics, originally due to take place from July 24 to August 9, 2020, was postponed immediately, marking the first time the Olympics has ever been postponed or rescheduled. Locally, Piedmonters looked forward to the July 4 parade, the biggest event in town; but the possibility of bringing in hundreds of attendees seemed inconceivable, and the parade in its traditional form of cars, people and floats, was cancelled. articles.text: I am so disappointed and frustrated to see the latest crop of obnoxious signs that have popped up around town (“Open our schools”, see March 10 Post front page article). In a town that prides itself on its beautiful parks and yards, as also featured in the March 10 Post, it is unbelievable how many signs have shown up in the last year – political signs that should have been removed months ago (per City code), BLM signs, “We believe in science”, Giving Campaign, Senior Class, Girl Scout cookies, plus the ongoing Covid warnings and usual contractor advertisements. Enough is enough. The Senior Class signs showed up in January, so they’ll be up until at least June; these “Open our schools” signs refer to fall classes, so they’ll be up until at least September. The proliferation of such blight not only detracts from the attractiveness of most yards but is also a distraction to drivers, who are constantly catching sight of them and taking their eyes off the road. Perhaps the most frustrating aspect is that the homeowners themselves who display these signs don’t have to look at them; rather, it’s the neighbors, walkers and drivers who are harassed by them. Not to mention the fact that I seriously doubt if anyone in the School District will be influenced by a street sign campaign. So, what is the point? Please respect your community and remove unnecessary signs – or, if you’re that passionate about an issue, put it on your own porch so you can look at it constantly instead of the rest of us. Thank you for your consideration of others. –Patricia Singer

articles.text: One new case of COVID-19 in Piedmont in March As Alameda County cautiously reopens, new cases of COVID-19 continue to drop according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in Alameda County dipped to 1.4 percent as of Monday, March 15. The positivity rate has not been this low since mid-October, when positivity rates dipped before a rapid winter surge of the disease. California moved Alameda County into the Red Tier for reopening its economy last Tuesday, March 9 as new cases of COVID-19 decrease in the area. The Red Tier, or Substantial Tier, is the second-most restrictive tier in the state’s four-tier color-coded metric. Before that, the county was in the Purple, or Widespread, Tier – the most restrictive tier. As of last week, indoor dining, movie theaters, museums and gyms reopened with capacity restrictions. Capacity restrictions on retail and grocery stores were reduced. Small private gatherings among no more than three households are permitted indoors, although gathering outdoors is strongly encouraged. Masks and distancing are required. As of yesterday, Tuesday, March 16, Alameda County meets all of the metrics to move into the Orange Tier, or Moderate Tier, the second-least restrictive tier. To move into the Orange Tier, the positivity rate needs to stay below 4.9 percent. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 3.9 – right now there are 3.6 cases per 100,000. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to be below 5.2 percent – it is currently 2.4 percent in Alameda County. In the Orange Tier, more indoor business operations are permitted with modifications. San Mateo County was moved into the Orange Tier by the state this week and is the only Bay Area county currently not in the Red Tier. Neither ACPHD nor the state have remarked on Alameda County’s status this week, but the state typically waits for a county to meet metrics for at least a week before moving them to a less-restrictive tier. One new case was reported in Piedmont over the past seven days, the first case in March recorded in the City. In total, there have been 168 cases reported in Piedmont. Across Alameda County, the total caseload for the county is 82,168. There have been 25,502 cases recorded in Oakland and 12,910 cases in Hayward. There have been 1,330 deaths caused by COVID-19 countywide. While many health experts are cautiously optimistic about the current course of the pandemic, there are calls for the public to remain vigilant with mask use and social distancing as new variants of COVID-19 are identified around the state. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,530,055 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 55,372 deaths due to the disease statewide.
articles.title: Alameda County meets Orange Tier metrics; stays in Red Tier for now

articles.text: Demand for vaccine continues to outstrip supply in Alameda County Even though Alameda County has not expanded eligibility for the COVID-19 vaccine to the extent allowed by California, almost half of Piedmont residents have received at least one dose of vaccine as of Sunday, March 14. On Monday, March 15, California permitted healthcare providers to vaccinate individuals ages 16 to 64 with certain health conditions that leaves them more at risk to COVID-19 mortality. However, as of press time, this additional group of people is not yet eligible in Alameda County. According to the Alameda County Public Health Department, the groups currently eligible for vaccination are based on age, employment and specific living situations. People aged 65 years and older have been eligible for weeks. Essential workers in healthcare, food, agriculture, education, childcare, emergency services, public transportation and air travel are now eligible. Additionally, those working or living in congregate living facilities, including people experiencing homelessness, are eligible. articles.text: The city has launched a community fair housing survey, which is accessible through its new “Piedmont is Home” website. The website will serve as a space for direct information from the city about a new housing policy in Piedmont, including project updates and public engagement opportunities. The website will focus on three main tenets of the city’s housing policy: • Senate Bill 2 Housing Programs Project • Measure A1 (Alameda County) grant • Update on the next Housing Element (2023–2031) Information and an FAQ (frequently-asked-questions) sample is available for each project. The website also includes an interactive “pinnable” map of Piedmont that asks users to place a pin in areas of the city that they believe could support more housing. Both the interactive map and the community fair housing survey were made accessible to residents on Friday March 12 and will be available until April 15. Completing the survey and “pinning” new housing sites on the map gives individuals a chance to win a $50 Mulberry’s Market gift card. The survey is one of several opportunities throughout the 18-month city-led effort to “ensure that new housing in Piedmont is feasible to develop, high in quality, affordable, and fits in the neighborhood context,” the website stated. The Piedmont is Home planning initiative will look specifically at multi-family housing, residential mixeduse development, and accessory dwelling units (ADUs) as avenues for affordable housing. The survey can be completed in 20-25 minutes. It is meant to walk any teacher, whether novice or veteran, through the necessary procedures on the all-important first day of school. Harry and his wife, Rosemary, are both teachers. Harry is a Bay Area native, a graduate of Lowell High School and UC Berkeley. He’s been awarded numerous accolades, including the Horace Mann Outstanding Educator Award, Upton Sinclair Award, Outstanding Secondary Teacher Award, the Science Teacher Achievement Recognition Award, the Outstanding Biology Teacher Award, and the Valley Forge Teacher’s Medal. Teachers have been using the “Wong Method” for decades because, in short, it works. Many teachers that I’ve spoken to say they followed The First Days of School religiously as novices, but then learned to tweak it and make it work for their teaching style and their students’ learning preferences. Of course, the text is often read in the summer, in preparation for the start of the academic year; but now with students returning to school in droves across the Bay Area, it never hurts to revisit a classic. In the first days and weeks it’s important to be accessible, positive, transparent, and clear in your expectations. “If you do not have a plan, you are planning to fail.” The Wong Method calls for procedure, routine, and planning. Getting back into some semblance of a routine will be difficult and not without practice. Parents of students in hybrid learning models should replicate a typical school day to the best of their abilities so that the eventual return to normalcy will not be such a shock. “Teachers + Parents = good students.” The Wongs were steadfast in their belief that name recognition matters and improves student focus. “Drop-off” and “pick-up” is also a valuable time to chat with parents – not necessarily about their child, but simply for both parties to be “available.” In a COVID world, students are shuffled from car to classroom in haste. While there may be no way around this for now, as a parent it is imperative that your child knows that you want to have a positive relationship with their teacher. After all, you both are a team. articles.text: Deadline to enter League of Women Voters contest is April 17 The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is sponsoring its second annual essay contest, open to all Piedmont high school juniors and seniors. The essay should answer the question, “Given the fragility of democracy as evidenced by the insurrection of January 6, 2021, how can your generation work to ensure that democracy in the United States is strengthened for future generations?” Contest entrants may, but are not required to, rely on outside sources that are properly cited within the text and in a bibliography. A specific format for citations or bibliography is not required, but there must be enough information to allow the judges to easily verify your sources. Citations do not count toward your total number of words. Remember that this essay is not solely a research paper and should draw on the writer’s personal experiences and insights. Essays will be judged on originality, clarity of expression, vocabulary and style, proper grammar, punctuation and spelling. Students are encouraged to have a teacher, parent or mentor review the essay prior to submission keeping in mind that all work must be the student’s own. The essay must be 250 to 500 words, excluding citations. At the top of the essay include the following information: the title, your first and last name, city of residence (must be Piedmont), name of your school, and your current grade. Essays must be typed and double-spaced and submitted in a .pdf format. All entries are to be submitted to lwvpiedmont@gmail.com. The deadline is April 17. Winners will be announced on May 1.

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Mock Trial team placed first at the Alameda County Philip A. Harley Memorial Mock Trial Competition on February 25, beating Bishop O’Dowd in the finals and advancing to the State competition. Led by history teacher and coach Dave Keller, Piedmont’s prosecution narrowly defeated O’Dowd’s defense, 772 to 761. The round was presided over by Judge Noël Wise from the Alameda County Superior Court and scored by a panel of five attorneys. Piedmont’s team was undefeated through the entire competition, which took place in January and February. In nearly two months of events, Piedmont beat Albany, Berkeley, Granada, and American high schools in the first four rounds and defeated Amador Valley in the semi-finals, 587 to 583. This marks the first time in over six years that PHS has won the Alameda County championship. The last time PHS competed in the county finals was 2018. Piedmont now advances to the state competition where it will represent Alameda County against other schools in California. Mock trial is a simulated trial competition based on the California criminal courts system. Each round requires about two hours. The Alameda County competition is named in memory of Philip Harley, a Piedmont resident and member of the Kazan Mcclain Satterley & Greenwood Law Firm.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team made short work of the visitors from Alameda on Saturday. March 13, sweeping their league opponent 6-0. The tam was set to face Bishop O’Dowd two days earlier, but the match was canceled due to complications in the Dragons’ athletic department. “To be honest, I was worried before the match [with Alameda] because we were missing about a quarter of the team due to a fourday weekend. I guess I didn’t need to be. We blanked Alameda without losing a single set,” said Piedmont coach Jim Landes. Junior Charlie Lambert made his second appearance at No. 1 singles under some interesting circumstances. “Charlie took the SAT in the morning but still came back clear-headed enough to defeat Alameda’s Mason Conlin 7-6 (7-5), 6-2. Charlie hit some fabulous forehands, big serves and played some great defense too,” said Landes. Senior Sajan Srivastava won at No. 2 singles in straight sets, 6-4, 6-4, while freshman Ben Breber won at No. 3 in a 6-1, 7-5 victory. Senior Luke Hawkins was in good form at No. 4 singles winning in straight sets. “Luke is already getting in his late-season form winning decisively with strong ground strokes mixed in with his signature slices and drop shots,” said Landes. In doubles, Landes had high praise for the three doubles teams, each of whom won in straight sets, and all three doubles teams holding Alameda to three or fewer points. “All three teams overwhelmed their opponents,” commented Landes. “One of the Alameda coaches told me our doubles players seemed to always know where they needed to be. articles.text: Boys win meet in Hercules; girls place third urday, March 13 in the Hercules Piedmont cross-country runners competed in a 4-school meet with league teams Berkeley, Castro Valley, and Alameda on Sathills. Competing in a field of 28 runners, PHS junior Ellie Black won the girls varsity race with a time of 19:45. It marked the second meet of the season for both the boys’ and girls’ teams. Stein’s 15:54 was an improvement of five seconds and a new PR for him. He was 11 seconds ahead of Alameda’s David Song, who placed 2nd. Their key player [Emerson Bohlig] is a Division 1 recruit to Northwestern and was really fast out there. Miramonte is a really good team,” said Piedmont coach Carlton Chan. Piedmont kept it close in the first half, down 9-5 at halftime but within striking distance. Caroline Devine scored the first goal of the game for Piedmont after a minute of play, but Bohlig scored four of her nine goals for a 4-1 lead after nine minutes. The Matadors never relinquished the lead. “Contributions from the defense again,” said Chan. “Maya Galbreth and Bella Kjellen did well on defense. They were the main duo on double teams, but with Miramonte moving the ball and their speed, we didn’t have enough to keep a constant double.” Piedmont had their chances on net, but Miramonte goalie Mina Jenab stuffed several shots. Katherine Kinne managed to score have a first half hat trick and Devine added a second goal, but the Matador defenders played well. “We played really well in the first half; we double-teamed Emerson and forced her to pass the ball. We left about four or five shots on the table,” explained Chan. “Sadie [Tschider] had some beautiful feeds, but their senior goalie stuffed us.” Miramonte came out on fire in the second half, holding Piedmont scoreless until five minutes were left in the game. Despite the loss, Chan have high praise for his team’s tenacity while playing undermanned. “With just 14 players and only three true midfielders, it was just difficult to keep up the intensity for a full match. Our ‘tenacity award’ goes to Eliza Keville, she gave their offense fits by knocking down balls and playing scrappy defense. We moved her to midfield with eight minutes left and she scored on a wonderful cut,” said Chan. Final stats include: Kinne with three goals, Devine with two goals and three assists, Tschider had one assist, and Keville had one goal. articles.text: Oakland Museum of California The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) is offering online exhibitions that celebrate Women’s History Month on the museum’s website. You can access the Dorothea Lange: Photography as Activism archive online at any time. A world-renowned documentary photographer, Lange played an instrumental role in humanizing the impact the Great Depression had on Americans in the 1930’s. Her photography was designed to provoke social and political change, and questioned the role or class, race, and justice in a growing country. You can explore her powerful work on OMCA’s Dorothea Lange Digital Archive at https:// dorothealange.museumca.org/. Works by Mine Okubo, Helen Nestor, Favianna Rodriguez, Hung Liu, and Faith Ringgold are also available to view. You can view all featured artists, all of whom have had their work showcased at OMCA, by visiting the museum’s website at https://museumca.org/blog/celebrating-womens-history-month-omca. An upcoming, in-person exhibit at OMCA is Mothership: Voyage into Afrofuturism, which features contemporary works such as a Dora Milaje costume from the Marvel comic film Black Panther, as well as author Octavia E. Butler, avant-garde jazz musician Sun Ra, and filmmaker Kahlil Joseph. Mothership offers a “powerful reason to gather and celebrate Black imagination.”

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum reopened to the public on March 7 following San Francisco County’s move to the less restrictive red tier. The museum offered free admission on its first day, and is showcasing a mix of old and new exhibitions; including some that ended abruptly due to the pandemic and subsequent museum closures one year ago. One of the current exhibitions, Zheng Chongbin’s “I Look for the Sky,” is an art installation using transparency and light to explore how ephemeral changes can alter the viewer’s perception of place. Also currently on view is “After Hope: Videos of Resistance,” an exhibition that showcases an eclectic selection of more than 50 short videos that “explore the role of hope in contemporary art and activism.” Chanel Miller’s “I was, I am, I will be” inaugural work is still available to view on the façade of the building, facing Hyde Street. The art installation represents healing in a three-part process: reflecting on the past, being mindful in the present, and envisioning the future. Growing up in Palo Alto, Miller said she frequented the museum but never dreamed that one day she would be featured. “Whenever I was upset, I’d take a sharpie to the wall and sit for hours and let these ‘creatures’ come to life. I could create landscapes that don’t have narrow borders. That’s the scene that came out of this feeling,” Miller said. Even though the museum’s doors were closed due to shelterin-place orders, Miller’s exhibit was visible without even setting foot into the building. At night, Miller’s black and white figures are illuminated and visible from the street. The Asian Art Museum is open 1 p.m. to 8 p.m. on Thursdays and 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday through Monday; the museum is closed on Tuesday and Wednesday. Reservations and timed ticketing is required, and tickets can be reserved at https://about. asianart.org/plan-your-visit/. The use of face masks and coverings and social distancing must be observed.
articles.title: Asian Art Museum reopens to the public

articles.text: San Francisco’s Museum of Modern Art Two weeks shy of a full year with its doors closed due to the COVID pandemic, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) announced on March 2, that it has reopened to the public following San Francisco County’s move to the less-restrictive Covid red tier. The museum officially opened with a Free Community Day and free parking on Sunday, March 7. The museum is reopening with a range of exhibitions, including Close to Home: Creativity in Crisis, which highlights seven local artists’ responses to a year of sheltering in place. Carolyn Drake, Rodney Ewing, Andres Gonzalez, James Gouldthorpe, Klea McKenna, Tucker Nichols, and Woody De Othello demonstrate a vast range of artistic, emotional and political responses. It will be on display until September 5. Off the Wall, also on display until September 5, shows five contemporary artists who transform one medium to another. Liz Deschenes, Oliver Chanarin, Sarah Sze, Dayanita Singh, and Lieko Shiga are the featured artists who transform photographic art into sculpture. Finally, New Work: Charles Gaines is a new installation of two major works that explore the history of racism in the United States. New Work begins with the 1857 Dred Scott Decision. “We are delighted to welcome our community back to SFMOMA after such a challenging year for so many,” said SFMOMA Director Neal Benezra. “Deep thanks to our dedicated staff, whose creativity helped keep our audiences engaged and inspired online during closure, and whose hard work enables us to safely reopen. We’re thrilled to provide safe and uplifting in-person art experiences in our spacious, airy galleries once again.” SFMOMA’s hours will be Friday through Monday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Thursdays from 1 p.m. to 8 p.m. SFMOMA is limiting the number of visitors each day to 25 percent of its regular capacity. Masks are required for all who enter the museum. For more information, visit https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/off-the-wall/.
articles.title: SFMOMA reopens to the public

articles.text: Photo by Erik Tomasson San Francisco Ballet dancers perform Ratmansky’s Symphony No. 9, part of the Shostakovich Trilogy. Choreographer Alexei Ratmansky’s Symphony No. 9, part of the Shostakovich Trilogy, will stream through March 24 as part of the San Francisco Ballet’s third digital program. Created for 21 dancers and performed in May 2019 at the War Memorial Opera House, Symphony No. 9 highlights two lead couples and a solo male, all set against designer George Tsypin’s backdrop of grays and reds, recalling works of Socialist realism, set to the music of composer Dmitri Shostakovich. The performance is an archival capture. Ratmansky had Russia in mind when he created the Shostakovich Trilogy, according to American Ballet Theater Ballet Master Nancy Raffa. “This is an homage to Shostakovich, because of Alexei’s enormous admiration for his talent and for what he symbolizes for Russian people,” she said. “But it’s also an homage to [Ratmansky’s] heritage. He grew up listening to and loving Shostakovich, so this was like a gift [to the composer]. And a gift to Russia.” In creating Symphony No. 9, Raffa said that Ratmansky considered the time the piece was written, and the emotions behind what was happening in Shostakovich’s life - the regime, the Communist party, and the “Stalin mentality.” “He wanted them to be almost a caricature, expressing the sarcasm in parts of the score. But everything is abstract. He kept saying, ‘There’s no story, but there’s a lot of meaning’,” Raffa said. To watch Symphony No. 9, visit https://www.sf ballet.org/ productions/digital-program-03/.
articles.title: SF Ballet streaming Ratmansky’s Symphony No. 9 through March 24

articles.text: In this pandemic era, it’s still feasible to produce ensemble music with eloquent messages, up to a point. For the S.F. Symphony’s latest SoundBox aphoristic set “Lineage” curated by mezzo Julia Bullock, a nonet performs under a conductor on a sound stage, assisted by a far-off chorus, with some musicians entering remotely via modern technology – with most of them well-spaced and masked. Welcome to the unique era of Covid and formats which will try many fans attempting to explain to baffled grandchildren many years hence. With the technology, Bullock assembled a moving and high-quality program appropriate to our unique times, lifting spirits and consoling, while showing creativity of several black artists and of women composers. In the 45 minutes of the streamed SoundBox format we get a mosaic of pieces small and even smaller, ranging from Bach to 12th-century hymns to poet Langston Hughes’ lament on behalf of “the sick, depraved,… all the scum.” Anyone accessing this “Lineage” program should know that the vocalist/pianist Simone was a heroic American figure of a half-century ago, battling discrimination while producing deeply affective songs that stand the test of time. All this is carried out with imaginative camera work (a mite too restless in its brief, shifty images) and artistic background projections. And when Bullock isn’t “taking the stage” from distant recording studios, we have conductor Daniel Stewart (of the Santa Cruz Symphony) leading ensembles in the late George Walker’s “Lyric for Strings” and an excerpt from Elizabeth Ogoneck’s “In Silence” with Benjamin Beilman on lead violin, backed by SF Symphony players. “Lineage,” a Soundbox discovery program, created by mezzo Julia Bullock, with members of the S.F. Symphony, streaming on https://www.sfsymphonyplus.org/products/lineage-julia-bullock, or on www. sfsymphony.org. For further info, call (415) 864-6000. Paul Hertelendy, a Piedmont resident, also writes reviews for www.artsSF.com. Mezzo soprano Julia Bullock It’s like digging into a bowl of mixed candies, only not as sugary. And Bullock’s bits-andpieces programming is superlative. If there is a more soulful mezzo than Bullock around these days, you have a long search ahead of you. She brings forth the depths of emotion and reflection with her keen musical sense and a voice even delving down in the contralto range for Nina Simone’s “Images” sung a cappella over a pedal-point held over from that 12th-century hymn by St. Hildegard – a brilliant juxtaposition that may have the latter composer smiling benignly from above.
articles.title: SF Symphony turns to streams in evolving format

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony has announced the launch of REAL Berkeley, a four-episode virtual film series that feature special guests from the Berkeley community, through curators, local videography, and chamber music performed by musicians of the orchestra. The series will begin Sunday, March 28 at 4 p.m. with writer and curator Kate Schatz. Schatz, originally from San Jose, is a feminist writer, activist, and educator. She is the creator of the Rad Women book series, along with illustrator Miriam Klein Stahl. Her children’s book, Rad American Women A-Z, was published by the well known Bay Area-publisher City Lights in Spring 2015, and spent a combined 11 weeks on the New York Times bestseller list. The first episode will feature three works by prominent female composers: Reena Esmail’s Meri Sakhi Ki Avaaz (My Sister’s Voice), Gabriella Smith’s Tessellations and Clara Shumann’s Piano Trio. The second episode will be released on May 16. REAL Berkeley is produced by Berkeley Symphony Artistic Director Rene Mandel, in partnership with Symphony Music Director Joseph Young and Bay Area-based media company Reneff-Olson Productions. The series will shine a light on the unique aspects of the city that Author Kate Schatz have had a positive and significant impact on both the orchestra, and its community members. “The importance of a strong and resilient community has been displayed throughout the past year as residents, businesses, organizations, and many others have all come together to provide support for one another during these difficult times,” Mandel said. “REAL Berkeley pays tribute to a community that we are proud to represent. We look forward to celebrating these wonderful aspects of our city through adventurous music and imagery that represent the diversity and ethos of Berkeley.” Visit https://www.berkeleysymphony.org/ for more information on how to watch the upcoming series.
articles.title: REAL Berkeley virtual film series begins March 28

articles.text: Each weekend in March, San Francisco Opera will stream soldout performances from the 2018 Ring Festival production for free. pages.text: Wednesday, March 17, 2021 17 By Paul Hertelendy In this pandemic era, it’s still feasible to produce ensemble music with eloquent messages, up to a point. For the S.F. Symphony’s latest SoundBox aphoristic set “Lineage” curated by mezzo Julia Bullock, a nonet performs under a conductor on a sound stage, assisted by a far-off chorus, with some musicians entering remotely via modern technology – with most of them well-spaced and masked. articles.text: Baykali Ganambarr and Aisling Franciosi star in The Nightingale. Film review by Chris Honoré I encourage you to not miss The Nightingale. I feel compelled to say that as a narrative it’s a hard watch. But know that it’s powerful, provocative, and filled with moments that bleed into every scene. The performances to a person are extraordinary. The setting is Tasmania. The year is 1825. A young Irish woman, Clare (Aisling Franciosi), an ex-convict, is awaiting parole having completed a seven-year sentence for a theft committed in Ireland. Her release, which she is desperate to obtain, is dependent on a British lieutenant Hawkins (Sam Claffin). He requires Clare, considered an indentured servant, to wait on his troops in barracks and entertain them with her beautiful voice, singing songs from the homeland (hence the title). And though married with a child in arms, she is forced to yield to his constant sexual assaults while remaining mute as she awaits her freedom. She also understands that should her husband find out, his reaction would put her release in jeopardy. It is at this point that two rending violations occur, both involving Hawkins. The second, an unbearably difficult scene to watch, results in an unimaginable loss for Clare. And it is this scene that frames the rest of the story. Learning that Hawkins has left on foot with some men for the north, where he anticipates securing a promotion, Clare, on the verge of madness, sets out on a journey of jaw-clenching revenge. This deeply damaged woman, who has known only oppression, realizes that she can’t make the trek through rugged and deeply forested terrain alone, and so hires an aboriginal tracker named Billy (Baykali Ganambarr) to guide her, following Hawkins’ trail. Together they forge a fragile alliance, their harrowing, unrelenting voyage taking them into the darkest places in the human heart. They are forced to face an unforgiving barbarity and racist malevolence, all too familiar, carried out by the British colonizers toward the aboriginal people with impunity. However, despite their grudging partnership and Clare’s deep need for help – Billy is fully aware of the danger they both face. It is only gradually, after a tortuous walkabout, that they come to rely on one another and find common ground and unexpectedly come to recognize in each other a mutual humanity that transcends their individual circumstances and histories. Powerlessness and oppression have been part of Clare’s life experience; and it is all Billy has ever known. But in one powerful scene, the sky above now dark, a pervasive sense of hopelessness griping them, Clare reaches out and takes Billy’s hand in her own acknowledging that where they have been and where they are now has been for both of them transformative. The Nightingale is a remarkable piece of filmmaking, and for all of its dark vision it is ultimately hopeful. At one point Clare and Billy stand on a stretching beach and watch as a rising sun fills the horizon. They find in this moment a negation of Clare’s earlier admonishment to Billy when she says, “Welcome to the world, boy, full of misery from top to bottom.” The Nightingale. Directed by Jennifer Kent. Starring Aisling Franciosi, Sam Claflin and Baykali Ganambarr. 2 hrs., 16 min. Rated R.

articles.text: Film review by Chris Honoré In retrospect, the Soviet Union and the United States managed to navigate almost 50 years of adversarial encounters without a confrontation that would have taken us past the brink of the deterrence known as mutual assured destruction (aka MAD). Part of the kabuki dance that the two superpowers engaged in, however, was based upon elaborate and sustained spying. Steven Spielberg’s Bridge of Spies, is a taut, well-made film based on a true story. It begins in 1957 with the arrest by the FBI of a Soviet spy, Rudolf Abel (Mark Ryance). The government, certain it has overwhelming evidence of his clandestine activity, decides to put him on trial. James Donovan (Tom Hanks), an insurance attorney, is selected to defend Abel who has stoically resisted all attempts by the CIA to extract information from him. What the government does not anticipate is that Donovan mounts a rigorous defense on Abel’s behalf, followed by an appeal of his conviction. Donovan was denigrated for carrying out what he felt was his constitutional obligation. He also suggested to the trial judge that Abel not be given the death penalty, arguing that should one of our spies be captured we just might need Abel should there be a proffered swap. So that’s the protracted set up. But Bridge of Spies, written by the award-winning writers and directors, brothers Joel and Ethan Coen, is a remarkable two-act story. Act one is the Abel capture and trial. Act two involves Donovan’s prescient statement about a possible trade at some point in the future – our guy for your guy. Our guy, as it turned out, was Francis Gary Powers, the U2 spy plane pilot, shot down in 1960 by the Russians. What could go wrong does go wrong. He is captured and put on trial. The Soviets now have their spy. This is a wonderful, spare, retro piece of moviemaking, delivered as only Spielberg can. Act two is launched. Donovan is selected to negotiate the exchange and arrives in East Germany just after the Berlin wall was built (1961) to talk to the Soviets and the East Germans about how to achieve the grudgingly agreed upon trade. It’s winter, the skies are leaden, East German buildings and streets are awash in institutional grays. Donovan, suffering from a tenacious cold, walks ever closer to a precipice, lost in a world of duplicity and obscure signals. He never knows if he is in discussion with the decision-makers or straw men. All that has occurred, from 1957 to 1962, leads to that intersection on a bridge which divides East from West. The outcome is always in doubt, the distrust between the players palpable. Tom Hanks gives a nuanced and spot-on performance. But not to forget Mark Ryance, accomplished stage actor, as Abe. His character is laconic in the extreme while laced with a humor so dry that it crackles. He is scene-stealing superb. As is this very entertaining film. The film won three Academy Awards in 2015: Best Performance by an Actor in a Supporting Role (Ryance); Best Motion Picture of the Year (Spielberg); and Best Writing, Original Screenplay (Coen brothers). Bridge of Spies. Directed by Steven Spielberg. Starring Tom Hanks, Mark Rylance and Alan Alda. 2 hrs., 21 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: Daisy Ridley and John Boyega star in The Force Awakens. Movie review by Chris Honoré Star Wars: The Force Awakens, released in 2015, is the seventh in what is one of the most successful franchises in film history. Over the decades – dating to the first release in May 1977 – the generic Star Wars has morphed into a cultural phenom, one that has captured the imaginations of moviegoers globally, even when the sequels and prequels didn’t quite reach the level of the initial trilogy (Star Wars IV: A New Hope, The Empire Strikes Back, and Return of the Jedi). Woven through all the Star Wars films is the question: what is there about these stories, these characters, that is so compelling and has consistently resonated with wide-ranging audiences, generating huge box office numbers? Perhaps the genius pf writer and original director George Lucas was in crafting a blend of high tech/low tech medieval lore (Princesses, Jedi Knights, mystical swords and dark Lords), combined with those mid-20th century Republic serials that kids flocked to every Saturday to watch cliff-hanging installments of action and adventure (Don Winslow of the Navy, Flash Gordon, or white hat/black hat westerns). And hands down, there’s never been a better example of a character from the dark side than Darth Vader (aka Lord Vader), his black mask menacing, covering a visage we can only imagine, every breath a wheezing sound, surrounded by armed stormtroopers. His persona – voice, stature – was inspired and breathtaking (pardon the pun). This was sci-fi fantasy unlike anything we had ever seen before. And so, began a narrative that would span three movies and would introduce a galaxy far, far away that was both myth and entertainment and proved to be irresistible. Ultimately, these films (to include The Force Awakens) are wonderfully constructed morality plays, primal fantasies that reduce our complex world, filled with ambiguity and uncertainty. They displayed good vs. evil, as exemplified by an outgunned Rebellion/Resistance struggling to defeat the forces of the Empire/The First Order. The loosely structured band of Rebels – never ominously militaristic – also represents the best impulses of men and women who yearn for Democracy. And they still possess those familiar X-Wing fighters, while remaining ready to confront Fascism’s jack-booted soldiers and their deadly armaments to include a Death Star equipped with a planet-destroying ray. Regarding this release, The Force Awakens, it is the first installment of a fresh trilogy that introduces a new generation of characters such as Rey (Daisy Ridley), a space junk scavenger; and Finn (John Boyega), a reluctant stormtrooper; as well as Poe Dameron (Oscar Isaac), a hotshot Resistance pilot sent in search of Luke Skywalker. And not to forget Darth Vader’s masked acolyte, Kylo Ren (Adam Driver), who kneels at the feet of the supreme leader, Snoke (Andy Serkis), one very large dude. The story manages to skirt a precipice of nostalgia while avoiding being maudlin as it builds a bridge between the original trilogy, featuring Han Solo (Harrison Ford), Princess Leia (Carrie Fisher), now a general in the Resistance, and at some point Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill). Clearly, the coming films will focus on what will be the ongoing battle, in all its permutations, between The Resistance and The Front. So, if The Force Awakens is considered in great part prologue, then some of the best is yet to come. In essence, it is the first reboot of the initial Star Wars and pays homage to those first three films that so completely solidified the brand (enough to survive Jar Jar Binks and company). For the proto fans who sat down for the first time, back in 1977, and watched the yellow block script scroll slowly into the dark distance, words that framed the battles ahead, well, even today that moment remains unforgettable, if not iconic. But that was then and this is now. Kids having that exact same experience with The Force Awakens won’t be disappointed. The force is beginning to awaken. Wait for it. Star Wars: The Force Awakens. Directed by J.J. Abrams. 2 hrs., 16 min. Starring Harrison Ford, Daisy Ridley and John Boyega. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: Film review by Chris Honoré Don’t let Wonder slip away without corralling the kids and taking them to see this remarkable film. It is a touching family narrative about a 10-year-old boy, Auggie (Jacob Tremblay), who since birth has suffered with a craniofacial, genetic disorder, an affliction that has distorted his face – he has endured some 27 surgeries. While at first blush it could be considered an early adolescent film, Wonder is so much more. It is life-affirming and brims with a surprising and unrelenting humanity. Auggie has always been homeschooled by his mom, Isabele (Julia Roberts). But now he finds himself confronting leaving the safety and embrace of his home and family – to include his father Nate (Owen Wilson) and his sister Via (Izabela Vidovic). He is about to begin his first year in middle school, a place where he will confront for the first time the judgment of his peers. As Isabel and Nate walk him to school, Isabel utters a quiet prayer, saying, “Please, don’t let the kids be cruel.” And yet she knows that by definition cruelty can define so many aspects of middle school. So, of course, Wonder is how Auggie strives to adjust to an environment for which he is profoundly unprepared. But to this film’s credit, it is never overly sentimental or maudlin; rather it inserts into the story other points of view. As example, Via, who for much of her life has felt on the periphery of the family, understanding intellectually that Auggie has required so much of her parents’ attention, yearns to find a closeness with her family that she has found to be elusive. Via’s perspective gives the movie a dimension that could easily have been left out. It brings to the film a conflicted complexity that adds to its sense of reality, one that is deeply humane. Wonder also doesn’t dwell on Auggie’s past medical experiences nor does a doctor appear to give sage diagnostic advice. This is a family’s story, one that is imperfect and at moments heart wrenching. But for all of its emotive power, it is also about the resilience of the human heart. For though Auggie is bright and understands the reactions of his fellow students to what they see, he also realizes that he is fearful and untrusting of anyone who approaches him with an outstretched hand. To its credit, Wonder is from the first frame understated. It is subtle and subdued. It gently presents its narrative and draws you not only into Auggie’s world but also into that of his family and thereby fashions a realm in which the audience is asked, repeatedly, to look beyond Auggie’s mask and see what is a mere shadow of who this young boy really is as he struggles with his isolation. It’s a wonderful movie going experience. There’s a line in the film that resonates from beginning to end: “When given a choice between being right and being kind, choose kind.” That alone sums up this film. Wonder. His persona – voice, stature – was inspired and breathtaking (pardon the pun). This was sci-fi fantasy unlike anything we had ever seen before. And so, began a narrative that would span three movies and would introduce a galaxy far, far away that was both myth and entertainment and proved to be irresistible. Ultimately, these films (to include The Force Awakens) are wonderfully constructed morality plays, primal fantasies that reduce our complex world, filled with ambiguity and uncertainty. They displayed good vs. evil, as exemplified by an outgunned Rebellion/Resistance struggling to defeat the forces of the Empire/The First Order. The loosely structured band of Rebels – never ominously militaristic – also represents the best impulses of men and women who yearn for Democracy. And they still possess those familiar X-Wing fighters, while remaining ready to confront Fascism’s jack-booted soldiers and their deadly armaments to include a Death Star equipped with a planet-destroying ray. Regarding this release, The Force Awakens, it is the first installment of a fresh trilogy that introduces a new generation of characters such as Rey (Daisy Ridley), a space junk scavenger; and Finn (John Boyega), a reluctant stormtrooper; as well as Poe Dameron (Oscar Isaac), a hotshot Resistance pilot sent in search of Luke Skywalker. And not to forget Darth Vader’s masked acolyte, Kylo Ren (Adam Driver), who kneels at the feet of the supreme leader, Snoke (Andy Serkis), one very large dude. The story manages to skirt a precipice of nostalgia while avoiding being maudlin as it builds a bridge between the original trilogy, featuring Han Solo (Harrison Ford), Princess Leia (Carrie Fisher), now a general in the Resistance, and at some point Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill). Clearly, the coming films will focus on what will be the ongoing battle, in all its permutations, between The Resistance and The Front. So, if The Force Awakens is considered in great part prologue, then some of the best is yet to come. In essence, it is the first reboot of the initial Star Wars and pays homage to those first three films that so completely solidified the brand (enough to survive Jar Jar Binks and company). For the proto fans who sat down for the first time, back in 1977, and watched the yellow block script scroll slowly into the dark distance, words that framed the battles ahead, well, even today that moment remains unforgettable, if not iconic. But that was then and this is now. Kids having that exact same experience with The Force Awakens won’t be disappointed. The force is beginning to awaken. Wait for it. Star Wars: The Force Awakens. Wonder a lovely story of a middle school boy Film review by Chris Honoré Don’t let Wonder slip away without corralling the kids and taking them to see this remarkable film. It is a touching family narrative about a 10-year-old boy, Auggie (Jacob Tremblay), who since birth has suffered with a craniofacial, genetic disorder, an affliction that has distorted his face – he has endured some 27 surgeries. While at first blush it could be considered an early adolescent film, Wonder is so much more. It is life-affirming and brims with a surprising and unrelenting humanity. Auggie has always been homeschooled by his mom, Isabele (Julia Roberts). But now he finds himself confronting leaving the safety and embrace of his home and family – to include his father Nate (Owen Wilson) and his sister Via (Izabela Vidovic). He is about to begin his first year in middle school, a place where he will confront for the first time the judgment of his peers. As Isabel and Nate walk him to school, Isabel utters a quiet prayer, saying, “Please, don’t let the kids be cruel.” And yet she knows that by definition cruelty can define so many aspects of middle school. So, of course, Wonder is how Auggie strives to adjust to an environment for which he is profoundly unprepared. But to this film’s credit, it is never overly sentimental or maudlin; rather it inserts into the story other points of view. As example, Via, who for much of her life has felt on the periphery of the family, understanding intellectually that Auggie has required so much of her parents’ attention, yearns to find a closeness with her family that she has found to be elusive. Via’s perspective gives the movie a dimension that could easily have been left out. It brings to the film a conflicted complexity that adds to its sense of reality, one that is deeply humane. Wonder also doesn’t dwell on Auggie’s past medical experiences nor does a doctor appear to give sage diagnostic advice. This is a family’s story, one that is imperfect and at moments heart wrenching. But for all of its emotive power, it is also about the resilience of the human heart. For though Auggie is bright and understands the reactions of his fellow students to what they see, he also realizes that he is fearful and untrusting of anyone who approaches him with an outstretched hand. To its credit, Wonder is from the first frame understated. It is subtle and subdued. It gently presents its narrative and draws you not only into Auggie’s world but also into that of his family and thereby fashions a realm in which the audience is asked, repeatedly, to look beyond Auggie’s mask and see what is a mere shadow of who this young boy really is as he struggles with his isolation. It’s a wonderful movie going experience. There’s a line in the film that resonates from beginning to end: “When given a choice between being right and being kind, choose kind.” That alone sums up this film. Wonder. articles.text: Fans of Botanical Garden raise $141,000 in Big Give campaign The University of California at Berkeley Botanical Garden set a goal of raising $65,000 in a 24-hour fundraising campaign. It announced that a total of 339 donors raised $141,714, far exceeding anyone’s expectation. The money will be used to restore the Tropical House (pictured). The Big Give is UC Berkeley’s annual campus-wide 24-hour fundraiser. This year’s campaign was held on March 11. A total of 15,991 gifts raised $11.8 million for the university, a portion of which are dedicated to UC Botanical Garden’s Tropical House restoration project. The Tropical House has been a main fixture in the garden for nearly 50 years. It has been a challenge to maintain throughout its history, however. Heating and irrigation systems in the house regularly failed, resulting in plant damage. More recently, glass panes cracked and fell, and engineers advised that the building required renovation and seismic retrofitting. The Tropical House was closed to the public in early 2020. “As the Tropical House structural improvements near completion, Garden staff see a new opportunity to renovate and refresh the house’s interior. UCBG Advisory Board member and well-known landscape architect Ron Lutsko is donating his firm’s services to design a modern interior that will engage and educate visitors with an intimate tropical experience. The project includes adding a shade strucUC Botanical’s Tropical House ture to the adjacent patio where small groups gather, and refreshing exterior plantings around the building,” Garden Director Lew Feldman said. Volunteer Mara Melandry agreed that the Tropical House needed a “major overhaul.” “The first phase was to reskin the entire building with polycarbonate material to replace the glass. This material does not need whitewashing and is twin-walled for greater insulation; other project elements included earthquake retrofitting and a new heating system to replace the ancient heaters. By August of 2020 the reskinning and earthquake retrofitting were in process. The next step is the redesign of the interior to enhance the visitor experience,” she said. For more information on the UC Botanical Garden and the tropical house, visit https://botanicalgarden.berkeley.edu/collections/tropical-house.
articles.title: UC Botanical Garden far exceeds goal in fundraiser

articles.text: It has been a challenging year. You don’t need me to tell you that. But all indications are telling us that things are looking up. With this in mind I suggested a mini vacation. Bodega Bay seemed to be ideal. I called a hotel which had been recommended to me. I asked for a modestly priced room. The manager said they had a room with a queen bed and a partial view… Modestly priced. “Six fifty” she said. That’s the way people talk today. In my day 650 meant six dollars and fifty cents. The manager reassured me that one night was actually $650. After overcoming my initial shock, I thanked her very much and decided on a different plan. My son invited me to lunch with him at a crêpe restaurant on Solano Avenue. Suzette Crêpe Café is a pleasant restaurant which offers a wide range of crepe possibilities. It is owned by a young Cambodian couple who really know what they’re doing. The husband does the cooking, and though born in Cambodia, he was raised in Normandy, France. After his parents were killed by the Khmer Rouge regime, he was adopted by a French couple. And Normandy is sort of the home of the crêpe. I chose a crêpe with Gruyere cheese, spinach and avocado. It was very good and had just the right amount of “al dente” as the Italians say. For dessert I had a coffee latte and a lemon crêpe with sugar butter and lemon juice. Everything was made to order – authentic and a very pleasant atmosphere. Feel free to engage the owners in a lively conversation. It was lots of fun. On Saturday my wife and I went to Speisekammer, the wellknown German restaurant in Alameda. It resembles an informal German countryside restaurant. Its owner is from the north of Germany but raised in Berlin. Some of the recipes come from his grandmother who grew up in the German area of Poland. Because of this I chose as my main course stuffed cabbage leaves with ground beef and a tangy herb sauce. My grandmother’s specialty was stuffed cabbage leaves. But those at Speisekammer are just about as good. The large portion priced at $21 gives you two large cabbage rolls and a large portion of mashed potatoes. We began the dinner with a superb red bell pepper soup, followed by a vegetable strudel. I enjoyed speaking with the owner, and some of the background music took me back to those exciting days when the Weimar Republic lead the world in all artistic things. Unpleasant truths It is interesting to contemplate what great musicians of the past would have to say about the present state of musical affairs. The publicity machines proclaim that these are the best of times and that no musicians have ever been better. As an historian I look back at what the geniuses of the past had to say, and I would also like Socrates to lead an open discussion. I’d like to have a Helios to shine light on the situation, and a Diogenes to look for some honesty and sincerity. It doesn’t matter where you look, the artists of today are all in a form of lockstep thinking. They attempt to justify everything they do. However, a philosophy of perpetrating erroneous facts and misconceptions is fallacy. When I challenge them and ask them why they do things, the response is always the same: “That’s the way they did it.“ This response is simply not true. Among earlier musicians, there was no uniformity... anywhere. The fact is that every country had its unique way of doing things. Every individual city had its unique way of doing things. And, furthermore there were individual styles of playing based on the precepts of your teacher.
articles.title: Six fifty

articles.text: H e l g i To m a s s o n h a s announced that he will conclude his tenure as Artistic Director and Principal Choreographer of San Francisco Ballet by mid- 2022. He has led the ballet company for nearly 40 years. “The unprecedented challenges we faced as individuals and as a community during 2020 only served to reconfirm for me the power of dance as a form of artistic expression, connection, and humanity,” he said. “Over the past ten months, we had to innovate and completely reconceive how to bring dance to our audiences, since they could not come to us. “Looking to the 2022 season, my aim is to build on these achievements and to bring the Company back to the stage for live performances. Because of the year we all lived through together, the Company has never been stronger than it is today. As we look ahead the timing felt right to begin a transition to a new Artistic Director, who will build on this legacy and lead the Company into its next chapter.” Tomasson was a distinguished dancer before assuming artistic leadership of San Francisco Ballet in 1985. Under his direction, the Ballet became a company widely recognized as one of the finest in the world. He has choHelgi Tomasson reographed more than 50 works for the Company, including fulllength productions of Swan Lake, The Sleeping Beauty, Romeo & Juliet (taped for Lincoln Center at the Movies’ Great American Dance), Giselle, and The Nutcracker (taped for PBS’s Great Performances). Tomasson has also connected San Francisco Ballet to the world, through co-commissions with American Ballet Theatre, The Royal Ballet, and Dutch National Ballet; and major tours to Paris, London, New York City, China, and his native Iceland. Last year, Tomasson was nominated to receive the San Francisco Arts Medallion, created by the Museum of Performance and Design to recognize those individuals whose leadership, action, and generosity have benefited the cultural life of the San Francisco Bay Area. The medal will be officially bestowed when in-person events can resume. “Helgi is a visionary whose creativity, brilliance, and stewardship of the Ballet is reflected both in the caliber of the Company’s work, as well as in the thoughtful transition plan that he helped conceive to support the organization’s ongoing vitality,” said Sunnie Evers, Co-Chair of the SF Ballet Board.

articles.text: Children’s Fairyland in Oakland Children’s Fair yland is reopening to the public this Friday, March 19, after a four-month closure due to COVID-19 health restrictions. The storybook theme park, located at Oakland’s Lake Merritt, has been closed since December 2020 due to Alameda County’s stay-at-home order. Now that the county has moved to the less restrictive “red tier,” Fairyland is ready to welcome guests once again. Per County guidance, the theme park will operate at reduced capacity with 1,000 attendees per day split between two sessions, mornings from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m., and afternoons from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m. These shifts will serve as two timed-entry sessions to ensure social distancing between guests. Masks are required for everyone over the age of two, and must be worn at all times, including when waiting in line for entry. The only exception is when you are in a designated eating area. The café will be open with a limited menu that is expected to expand this summer. The indoor gift store is now open, and visitors will be allowed to enter one “social bubble” at a time. Fairyland encourages guests to order from the retail store online. Rides, puppet shows, and other entertainment will resume when Alameda County enters the “orange tier.” This includes the Jolly Trolly, Wonder-Go-Round, Anansi’s Magic Web, and the Flecto Carousel. On Sunday, March 21, the afternoon shift is available for Fairyland members only. The park is currently open three days a week, Friday through Sunday. Beginning March 31, the park will be open five days a week. Fairyland will be open all week beginning June 7. Tickets are available online now at https://childrensfairyland. brushfire.com/fairyland. Guests must reserve tickets in advance.
articles.title: Children’s Fairyland reopens this Friday

articles.text: If you’re a brand-new parent, or even if you’ve been one for a little while, you’re no doubt filled with the many joys your child brings you. But as caught up as you are with the feelings and experiences of today, you also need to think about the future – specifically, the financial issues that accompany a growing family. What are some of the key moves you need to make? Here’s “checklist” to consider: • Establish a budget If you’re going to meet the additional expenses of a child, plus make progress toward other objectives, such as paying down debts, you’ll need to know where your money is going. Setting a budget, and sticking to it, may seem difficult, but once you’ve gotten into the habit, it will become easier – and for many people, following a budget actually gives them more of a sense of control over their finances. Over time, expenses related to your children will change, so you’ll need to adjust your budget accordingly – for example, once a child is in school full-time, childcare expenses may drop, which could allow you to boost your savings. • Protect against the unexpected If something were to happen to you, how would your child, or children, be affected? Even a family with two working parents can face serious financial difficulties if one of the parents were to die prematurely, or even just drop out of the workforce temporarily due to illness or injury. To help ensure your family could still stay in your home and your children could still afford to pursue higher education, you’ll want to create an appropriate protection strategy involving both life and disability insurance. Your employer may offer both, but the coverage provided may not be sufficient for your needs, so you may need to purchase your own policies. And here’s another protection-related idea: Try to build an emergency fund containing three to six months’ worth of living expenses, with the money held in a low-risk, liquid account. Without such a fund, you might have to tap into your longer-term investments to pay unexpected costs, such as a major car repair. • Prepare for high cost of higher education You may already be thinking about sending your child to college. Without such a fund, you might have to tap into your longer-term investments to pay unexpected costs, such as a major car repair. • Prepare for high cost of higher education You may already be thinking about sending your child to college. And it is indeed a good idea to start planning early because college is expensive, and it’s getting more so every year. However, you can prepare for these expenses through a college-savings vehicle, such as a 529 plan. A financial professional can help you pick the investment, or investment strategy, that’s appropriate for your needs. But whatever route you decide to follow, you won’t want to wait until your child is close to college age. • Keep long-term goals in mind Even while planning for the costs associated with raising a child, including saving for college, you can’t forget your other longterm goals. It isn’t selfish to build resources for your own retirement – in fact, you’ll ultimately be helping your family greatly by taking steps to maintain your financial independence throughout your life. So, during your working years, try to consistently contribute as much as you can afford to your IRA and your 401(k) or other employer-sponsored retirement plan. Having a child is obviously a life-changing event, and one with considerable financial challenges. But they can be manageable if you make the right moves at the right times. articles.text: Dr. Joel Parrott has announced that he will retire this spring after serving 37 years as President and Director of the Oakland Zoo. After three years of working as a veterinarian at the zoo from 1981- 1984, he was handed the reigns as the zoo’s new Director. Over a span of nearly four decades, Parrot has transformed the Oakland Zoo into a shining model of excellence, now world renowned. “After 37 years, my time has come,” Parrott said with a smile. “I have been working towards a goal for so long, right from high school. Really, there’s nothing like liberty and freedom.” Wearing his signature Australian bush hat, Dr. Parrott speaks at the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the Karibu Village in 2000. He has not only built up the zoo but has established a great legacy with the conservation and educational programs. The Oakland Zoo is a real leader.” In 2018 the zoo expanded its acreage for animal exhibits from 45 to 100 by adding the California Trail high atop the Oakland Hills with a majestic view of the Bay, accessible via a new gondola. With a Bachelor of Science and Doctorate in Veterinary Medicine degrees from Colorado State, he took on a zoo struggling financially in 1984 to its current $22 million dollar budget. “Joel had a tremendous impact on the zoo during his long tenure. He brought the zoo from a place where it had many deficiencies to a place where it is one of the most outstanding zoos in the country,” said Michael Bruck, former Piedmont Mayor and a member of the Oakland Zoo board. Dr. Parrott gives a medical exam to an otter in 1988. An extensive interview with Dr. Parrott revealed his passion and thoughtfulness. An extract from an interview conducted on February 25 follows. Q: How did you get started with the zoo? A: I went to Colorado State Veterinary School, then did an internship at the Denver Zoo kind of for fun and developed a specialty in wildlife. While working as a Wildlife Vet in Castro Valley for four years, the zoo contacted me to take care of the animals in 1981. familiar enough with the zoo and became restless with private practice. I decided to come on as Assistant Director and Veterinarian. A year later I became the Director. I was hired by William Penn Mott, who went from part-time Director of the Oakland Zoo to Washington D.C. as the Director of the National Park Service. Mott was already connected with Ronald Reagan when Reagan was California’s governor. So when Reagan became president, Mott was tapped to become the head of all 385 parks in the National Park Service. Q: What advice would you give to yourself 40 years ago when you first started? A: Be prepared for a long haul. Be prepared, for “anything may happen!” It actually became something I thrived on. I really liked not really knowing what was going to happen next. I hate routine jobs. So, if you want something where you are always having to be mobile and flexible and make adjustments on the fly, this is the job. Q: What conservation efforts are you most proud of? How has the zoo’s involvement in different conservation organizations evolved? A: We now take ourselves so seriously about conservation; we actually changed the name of our non-profit organization that runs the zoo. It used to be the East Bay Zoological Society. About three years ago we saw that our members spanned across the whole West Coast. More than just taking care of the Oakland Zoo, we are also here to protect. To more accurately reflect who we are, we changed our name to the Conservation Society of California. The name really reflects our identity and our mission. We previously never had a conservation program. We support 25 different non-profit organizations around the world and actively participate with them. Fifty cents of every admission goes to conservation. When you visit the Oakland Zoo you are contributing to conservation. articles.text: The Kistler family recently lost its cherished patriarch. Henry B, (Harry) Kistler died recently at the grand age of 98. He was a father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, yet so much more. Reflecting on his life, Harry often said, “I don’t know how one person can be so lucky.” Born in 1922, Harry attended the Le Rosey School in Switzerland, Phillips Exeter Academy in New Hampshire, and had just started his freshman year at Yale when World War II broke out. During the war, he served as a submariner in the Pacific. After the war ended, Harry resumed his studies at Yale, playing hockey and earning an undergraduate degree in Chemical Engineering. He went on to earn a graduate degree in Chemical Engineering at the University of Cincinnati. In 1949, Harry joined the Bechtel Corporation where he spent his entire 37-year professional career in a variety of positions including Project Engineer and Project Manager in the Engineering, Business Development, and Project Management departments. His work took him to Kuwait and other countries around the globe. Harry inherited a true love of sports from his father, an All-American football player in college. Harry loved skiing and spending time in the mountains. As a young father, he taught all his children how to ski on the slopes around Lake Tahoe. If snow had fallen the night before, 1946 and they had six children: Stephen, Henry, David, John, Lisa, and Maria. He was always a steady, guiding force in each of their lives. Years later, Harry met and fell in love with Ardagh Marie Veitch and they married in 1971. Ardagh Marie’s three children, Blake, Roxanne, and Edward, joined the large Kistler family, and Harry welcomed them with open arms. Each year, Ardagh Marie and Harry’s Christmas parties were the highlight of the holiday season for family and countless friends over several decades. Harry’s upbeat, positive personality was infectious and won everyone over. His winning smile, hearty laugh, strong hugs, powerful handshakes, and joy for living made everyone want to be in his presence. Harry is predeceased by Ardagh-Marie, who died three years ago. His memory will endure forever in the lives of his children, his 10 grandchildren, and three great-grandchildren. It is time to say goodbye and thank you to a well-loved and well-lived man. articles.text: Photo by Brian Mahany A large Japanese Maple can be viewed next to the Tea House in Piedmont Park. Heritage Tree nominations are due this Friday, March 19. The Heritage Tree program is an opportunity for the community to seek out and to recognize the distinctive trees in Piedmont’s urban forest. Nominated trees will be considered based on their aesthetic, educational, or historical merits and must grow on public property, such as parks, medians, and streets. An example of a Heritage Tree with excellent aesthetics is the stunning large Japanese Maple, Acer palmatum, next to the Tea House in Piedmont Park. It was nominated by Eileen Ruby in 2020. Japanese Maples have been cultivated in Japan for hundreds of years and around the world since the early 1800s. Some are shrub sized, while others can grow to a height of over 30 feet. They can be upright or weeping and have palmately lobed leaves that vary widely in shape and color. Most have vibrant fall colors. A Japanese Maple is a lovely focal point in any park, garden or patio. They can be grown in large containers and make excellent bonsai trees, although they otherwise do not require pruning. The 2021 Heritage Trees will be announced at the Park Commission hearing on April 7 and honored at this year’s virtual Arbor Day celebration on April 30. To nominate a tree, complete the downloadable form on the City’s website, https:// piedmont.ca.gov/government/ city_news___notifications/heritage_tree_nominations_open, For more information, contact Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov or call 510-420-3064.
